newsitem.title: USA: Republicans say Clinton blocks drug report.
newsitem.headline: Republicans say Clinton blocks drug report.

text.p: House Republicans Tuesday accused the Clinton administration of blocking a critical report on its anti-drug policy, but a Democrat said the charge was just a partisan election year attack.

The clash came at a House Government Reform subcommittee hearing on a report by the private Institute for Defence Analyses which found that interdiction was a better way to cut cocaine use than treatment of addicts.

The authors of the report, which was commissioned by the Defence Department, testified that they were called to the office of White House Drug Policy Director Barry McCaffrey in May to give him a briefing, but were told McCaffrey did not want to hear them because he disagreed with their conclusions.
"He (McCaffrey) instructed the study be quashed. The study showed the failure of the Clinton policies in the past three years," Florida Republican Representative John Mica said.
"This is just the latest chapter in the administration's attempt to explain away a major policy failure," said Committee Chairman William Clinger, a Pennsylvania Republican.
McCaffrey denied suppressing the report, which has not been completed or officially released. He said independent reviews found the report was badly flawed.
"None of us intended to repress or delay," he testified. "I didn't like it (the report)."
Clinton cut funding for interdiction of drugs before they reach the United States in favour of prevention and treatment programmes.
Maryland Democrat Elijah Cummings called the hearing, "Just another partisan attack on the administration's drug polices shortly before the election."
Republican presidential nominee Bob Dole and other Republicans have accused Clinton of ignoring the drug problem while drug use among U.S. teenagers rose sharply.

Barry Crane, one of the authors of the report, said the report was in its fourth draft and would be revised further. He said he stood by its findings, but added, "We do need to make some improvements in exposition."
Rex Rivolo, who also worked on the report, said he was upset when McCaffrey refused to hear their briefing. "I was angry. This is important information. We felt ignored."
Crane, Rivolo and Gary Comfort, the third author, said they had no evidence McCaffrey tried to suppress the report.

Separately, Clinger said the White House had invoked executive privilege to reject a committee subpoena for a memo from FBI Director Louis Freeh and Drug Enforcement Administrator Thomas Constantine on drug policy.
White House Counsel Jack Quinn said in a letter the memo was a confidential communication within the executive branch of government. Clinger said the memo criticised administration drug policy.
